query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Ti with Sc in the HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce the overall alloy density while preserving its high mechanical strength at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (around 1000°C).
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³ and excellent strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Replace Ti with Sc (e.g., form HfMoScTaZr by a partial or full substitution of Ti with Sc) during alloy fabrication.
generation.conditions: Mechanical performance characterized at room temperature and under high-temperature loading approaching 1000°C, using similar casting and heat-treatment protocols as the baseline alloy.
generation.structural_mediator: The substitution is expected to maintain the single-phase solid solution (likely BCC) and similar lattice distortions. The lighter Sc atoms lower the average atomic weight of the alloy without significantly altering the crystal structure.
generation.mechanism: Sc has a lower atomic weight compared to Ti, so replacing Ti with Sc reduces the overall density of the alloy. Simultaneously, the solid-solution strengthening effect and the distortion of the lattice are preserved, retaining comparable yield strength and high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Sc-substituted alloy should exhibit a lower density (less than 10.21 g/cm³) while maintaining yield strength and ductility within an acceptable margin (e.g., within 10% of the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr values) at both room temperature and around 1000°C.
generation.baseline: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr with density ~10.21 g/cm³ and high strength performance across room and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: Temperature range from room temperature up to approximately 1000°C under typical compressive/tensile loading conditions used in high-temperature structural applications.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of density reduction and the degree to which the mechanical properties are preserved depend on factors such as the homogeneity of Sc distribution, the potential for secondary phase formation, and processing conditions. These remain to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy samples using vacuum arc melting: one as the baseline HfMoTaTiZr and one where Ti is substituted fully or partially by Sc to form HfMoScTaZr. Apply identical homogenization heat treatments. Characterize both alloys using X-ray diffraction (XRD) to confirm a single-phase solid solution, scanning electron microscopy (SEM)/energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) for microstructure and compositional uniformity, and measure densities via Archimedes’ method. Conduct mechanical tests (tensile and/or compressive) at room temperature and at approximately 1000°C to assess yield strength, ductility, and overall performance.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sc-substituted alloy does not achieve a statistically significant reduction in density relative to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr (e.g., remains within 5% of 10.21 g/cm³) or if its yield strength and ductility at room temperature and ~1000°C deviate by more than roughly 10% from the baseline values, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

For examples, in 2010, the first RHEA, NbMoTaW RHEA, was fabricated by Senkov. The yield strength of NbMoTaW RHEA at 1600 °C is 405 MPa, and the working temperature limit of 1600 °C is much higher than that of nickel-based high temperature alloys about 1300 °C. In Xia’s study, the thermal stability of MoNbTaVW RHEA thin film was studied, and the experimental results show the body-centered cubic solid solution phase of MoNbTaVW RHEA is still very stable up to 1800 K. In Zhang’s experimental study, the plastic deformation mechanism of MoNbTaVW RHEA under high pressure was observed. It was found the active dislocation growth is mainly responsible for the high strength in the MoNbTaVW RHEA.
